subject: system-design
title: CAP and PACELC
summary: When the network splits, a distributed store must choose between staying consistent and staying available — and even when it doesn't split, it's still trading latency for consistency.

blocks.text: The CAP theorem describes a tension in any distributed data store across three properties: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system keeps working when the network drops messages between nodes).
The real choice is C vs A

In a distributed system, network partitions are not optional — links fail, so partition tolerance is a given, not a choice. That means when a partition happens, you must decide between two responses: refuse to answer until you can be consistent, or answer anyway and risk being stale.

items: CP — during a partition, sacrifice availability to stay consistent (reject or block requests). HBase and ZooKeeper-style systems lean this way.
AP — during a partition, sacrifice consistency to stay available (serve possibly stale data). Cassandra and Dynamo-style systems lean this way.
The choice can be per-operation: the same store may answer one query CP and another AP.

blocks.title: 'Pick 2 of 3' is wrong
blocks.text: CAP is often taught as choosing two of three properties, as if you could drop partition tolerance. You can't — partitions happen to you. The genuine choice is only between C and A, and only while a partition is in effect.
Most of the time there's no partition
Partitions are rare. CAP says nothing about the normal case, which is when your system actually spends almost all its life. That gap is what PACELC fills in.

PACELC reads: if there's a Partition, trade Availability vs Consistency (the CAP case); Else, trade Latency vs Consistency. Strong consistency requires coordinating replicas on every read or write, and that coordination costs latency — so even on a healthy network you're choosing how fresh data must be versus how fast you answer.

Classify a store by both clauses: a Dynamo-style system is PA/EL (available under partition, low-latency otherwise), while a strongly consistent store is PC/EC (consistent in both cases, paying latency for it).
